topics: 🗣️ Hearsay Testimony — may 'a witness in the name of a witness' permit a firstborn's slaughter?
⚖️ Rabban Gamliel vs. Rabbi Yehoshua — the famous public dispute over a scholar-priest's credibility
🐑 'An Israelite Gave It to Me Already Blemished' — when is a priest's claim believed?
🌾 Everyone Is Trusted About the Tithe's Blemishes — because the owner could have blemished the whole flock
👥 Three Laymen or One Expert? — a new mishna on who may certify a clear-cut blemish

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Layers of Trust in Certifying a Blemish
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 36a–36b
overview.hebrewSource: נֶאֱמָן הַכֹּהֵן לוֹמַר: הֶרְאֵיתִי בְּכוֹר זֶה וּבַעַל מוּם הוּא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Building on the question of whose testimony is trusted about a firstborn's blemish, the Gemara asks whether hearsay evidence suffices, tells the dramatic story of Rabban Gamliel publicly overruling Rabbi Yehoshua on a credibility question, and examines exactly which of a priest's claims are believed and which are suspect. A mishna then broadens the picture: unlike priests regarding a firstborn, everyone — even the owner — is trusted about a blemish on an animal tithe offering, since he could have achieved the same result legitimately. The daf closes with a new mishna asking whether three ordinary laymen, or only a trained expert, may certify that a blemish is severe enough to permit slaughter.

slides.title: 🗣️ Is Hearsay Testimony Valid for a Firstborn?
slides.subtitle: Rav Asi and Rav Ashi disagree over 'a witness in the name of a witness'

lines.speaker: Rav Asi
lines.text: Hearsay testimony (עֵד מִפִּי עֵד) may not permit a blemished firstborn's slaughter — a baraita limits such testimony to a woman testifying her husband died.

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi
lines.text: Emend the baraita: hearsay is valid for any matter where a woman's own testimony would be valid — and a firstborn's blemish is exactly such a matter.

lines.speaker: Rav Yeimar
lines.text: Ruled leniently in practice — earning the nickname from Mareimar, 'Yeimar who permits firstborns.'

callout.label: Halakha:
callout.text: The Gemara concludes that hearsay testimony is indeed valid for certifying a firstborn's blemish.

slides.title: ⚖️ The Public Dispute: Did We Distinguish Scholar from Ignoramus?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Tzadok's split lip becomes a test of rabbinic authority itself

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Tzadok's firstborn split its lip while eating barley. He asks Rabbi Yehoshua: was it ruled that a learned priest (חָבֵר) is trusted about his own blemish, unlike an ignoramus? Rabbi Yehoshua says yes
2️⃣ Rabbi Tzadok then asks Rabban Gamliel the same question — Rabban Gamliel says no such distinction was made, contradicting what Rabbi Yehoshua said
3️⃣ Before the assembled scholars, Rabban Gamliel confronts Rabbi Yehoshua directly, demanding he stand and be held to his earlier ruling

4️⃣ Rabbi Yehoshua concedes: 'Now that I am alive and he is alive, how can the living contradict the living?' He stands in submission until the crowd, offended by Rabban Gamliel's treatment of him, stops the lecture

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Whether a learned priest's greater credibility about his own firstborn's blemish is an established halakha or not — a dispute that spilled into a test of communal authority.

slides.title: 🐑 Which of the Priest's Claims Are Believed?
slides.subtitle: The mishna and Rav's extension, tested against real cases
rows: "I showed it to an expert; he ruled it blemished"
He would never risk eating sacrificial meat outside the Temple without real proof — karet is at stake
"An Israelite gave me this firstborn already blemished"
Any claim easily checked against the named Israelite tends not to be a lie
A priest lied with this very claim, but Rafram (the actual giver) recognized the animal and exposed him
The Gemara concludes this was one impudent exception, not grounds to distrust all priests generally

callout.label: Clear-cut exception:
callout.text: For an obvious, natural-looking blemish (like one eye larger than the other), Rav Ashi rules there is no concern at all — priest or Israelite, the blemish speaks for itself.

slides.title: 🌾 New Mishna: Everyone Is Trusted About the Tithe
slides.label: Why the tithe is different:
slides.text: Unlike a firstborn, where a priest benefits from a blemish and is therefore suspect, even the owner of an animal tithe offering is believed when he reports its blemish — because he could have legitimately caused a blemish in his entire flock before the tithing process began. Since 'He shall not distinguish between good and bad' (Leviticus 27:33) bars picking out the tenth animal in advance, there is no special incentive to lie about any one animal specifically.

slides.title: 👥 New Mishna: Who May Certify a Clear-Cut Blemish?
slides.subtitle: A blind eye, severed leg, or broken leg — obvious blemishes, but who may rule on them?

nodes.content: ❓ A firstborn's eye is blinded, foreleg severed, or hind leg broken — clearly permanent blemishes. Who may permit its slaughter?

columns.label: First tanna
columns.content: Three ordinary synagogue-goers suffice for such clear-cut blemishes

columns.label: Rabbi Yosei
columns.content: Even a court of twenty-three is not enough — only a true expert may rule

nodes.content: 🌍 Extended outside Eretz Yisrael: three laymen may permit a firstborn there too — but only for clear-cut blemishes (Rava)
📍 Further refined: three laymen suffice specifically where no expert is available; where an expert IS present, his ruling is required

callout.label: Parallel drawn:
callout.text: Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram compares this to dissolving a vow: three laymen suffice where no qualified Sage is present.

summary.principle: Whose testimony about a firstborn's blemish is trusted depends on incentive and verifiability — hearsay can suffice, a priest's claim about a named Israelite's gift is believed, and even three ordinary laymen may certify an unmistakable blemish when no expert is available.

flowSteps.content: 🗣️ Hearsay testimony is ultimately accepted to certify a firstborn's blemish
⚖️ Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua clash publicly over whether a learned priest is more trusted than an ignoramus

columns.content: 🐑 A priest's claim naming the Israelite who gave him the blemished animal is believed
🌾 Any owner is trusted about a tithe's blemish, since he could have blemished the whole flock legitimately

flowSteps.content: 👥 Three laymen may certify a clear-cut blemish where no expert is present; an expert is required where one is available
🎓 Key Principle: credibility tracks whether a claim is easily checked and whether the claimant stands to gain unfairly from a lie

quiz.q: What does the Gemara conclude about hearsay testimony ('a witness in the name of a witness') regarding a blemished firstborn?
o: It is never valid for any purpose
It is valid to permit the firstborn's slaughter, following Rav Ashi's reading of the baraita
It is valid only if the witness is a woman
It requires four witnesses instead of two
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes the halakha follows Rav Ashi: hearsay testimony is valid wherever a woman's own testimony would be valid, which includes a firstborn's blemish.

quiz.q: In the story of Rabbi Tzadok's firstborn, what did Rabban Gamliel do after Rabbi Yehoshua was forced to publicly admit his earlier ruling?
o: He apologized immediately and sat Rabbi Yehoshua down
He continued lecturing while Rabbi Yehoshua remained standing, until the people made him stop out of outrage
He reversed his own position on the matter
He expelled Rabbi Yehoshua from the study hall
quiz.e: Rabban Gamliel kept lecturing while Rabbi Yehoshua stood in forced deference, until the assembled people, offended by this treatment, told the disseminator to stop.

quiz.q: Why is a priest believed when he claims 'an Israelite gave me this firstborn animal with its blemish already on it'?
o: Priests are never suspected of lying about anything
Because the claim names a specific Israelite whose account could be checked, and people generally do not lie about matters likely to be revealed
Because the mishna requires no verification at all for such claims
Because only the Israelite's testimony matters, not the priest's
quiz.e: The principle 'any matter likely to be revealed, people do not lie about' underlies Rav's ruling — since the named Israelite could be questioned, the priest's claim is trusted.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, why is everyone — even the owner — trusted to testify about a blemish on an animal tithe offering (ma'aser behema), unlike a firstborn?
o: Because the tithe has no sanctity at all
Because the owner had no special incentive to lie, as he could have legitimately caused a blemish in his entire flock before the tithing process began
Because tithe animals cannot be blemished
Because only priests may own tithe animals
quiz.e: Since 'He shall not distinguish between good and bad' bars pre-selecting the tenth animal, the owner has no special motive to secretly blemish just one animal — he could have blemished the whole flock beforehand if he wished.

quiz.q: In the new mishna about clear-cut blemishes (a blinded eye, severed foreleg, broken hind leg), what is Rabbi Yosei's position?
o: Three laymen always suffice, even for uncertain blemishes
Even a court of twenty-three judges is insufficient — only a true expert may rule on the blemish
No blemish may ever be certified by anyone
Only priests may certify blemishes
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei disagrees with the first tanna and holds that even a large court cannot substitute for a genuine expert's ruling, even for seemingly obvious blemishes.
